title: Proteinuric renal disease with inconsistent autoimmune and clonal clues
summary: A woman in her 70s was referred for urgent outpatient review from respiratory clinic with dyspnoea and oedema. Her background included cystic lung disease without a known genetic variant, hypertension, vascular disease with previous coeliac artery stenosis and left vertebral artery dissection, obstructive sleep apnoea, and eclampsia with her second child.
purpose: Initial serology, renal pathology and protein studies do not point neatly to one cause. A later autoimmune association would not establish renal causation.
source_note: The visible packet stops at the post-biopsy assessment point. The three-month serial protein results, the later ptosis, negative receptor antibodies, single-fibre electromyography and the subsequent clinical course are withheld as hidden material. The source paragraph p-8 mixes initial and three-month data; only the initial values are presented as visible facts, and the packet flags the constructed selected-record nature of the review. The documented provisional diagnosis of idiopathic C3-dominant icMPGN is preserved as provisional, not promoted to certain. Source-audit corrections removed retrospective interpretation or hidden-result hints before answer generation; original preparation outputs remain preserved.

prepared_template.title: Proteinuric renal disease with inconsistent autoimmune and clonal clues
prepared_template.facts:
A woman in her 70s was referred for urgent outpatient review from respiratory clinic with dyspnoea and oedema. Her background included cystic lung disease without a known genetic variant, hypertension, vascular disease with previous coeliac artery stenosis and left vertebral artery dissection, obstructive sleep apnoea, and eclampsia with her second child.

On examination she was hypertensive, up to 207/81 mmHg, saturating 100% on room air, with a clear chest but raised jugular venous pressure and severe peripheral oedema to the level of the inguinal ligament.

Initial biochemistry: creatinine 158 µmol/L, urea 23 mmol/L, albumin 30 g/L. Urine albumin–creatinine ratio 232.3 mg/mmol, protein–creatinine ratio 332 mg/mmol, and 64×10^6/L dysmorphic erythrocytes on microscopy and culture. Coagulation showed no coagulopathy with an INR <0.9.

Autoimmune serology at initial assessment: ANA titre 1:640 with a homogenous pattern, but anti-dsDNA 3 IU/mL (normal <7 IU/mL). Myeloperoxidase-ANCA, proteinase 3-ANCA and anti-GBM antibodies were all negative. C3 was 1.20 g/L and C4 0.30 g/L, both within the normal range.

Infection and clonal screening at initial assessment: hepatitis C, HIV, hepatitis B surface antigens and core antibodies were negative. ASOT and Quantiferon gold were negative. Cryoglobulins were not detected. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrated a small IgG (kappa) band of trace amount on a background of an oligoclonal pattern; serum kappa/lambda ratio was 1.54 and urine Bence-Jones proteins were negative.

Complement dysregulation testing recorded around this evaluation: C3 nephritic factor was negative and genetic testing was negative for identified mutations in the CFHR3/1 and CFB genes. The source reports these alongside the initial investigations; the exact sampling dates relative to the biopsy are not separately stated, so this is a constructed selected-record review.

Imaging: ultrasound of the renal tract confirmed normal appearances of both kidneys. CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis did not demonstrate any occult infection, malignancy or thymoma.

Renal biopsy (22 glomeruli, 1 globally sclerosed): diffuse glomerular enlargement with increased mesangial and endocapillary cellularity and accentuated tuft lobularity. Silver staining showed increased mesangial matrix, glomerular basement membrane double contouring and mesangial cell interposition. Mesangial and intramembranous fuscinophilic deposits were present. There were no glomerular necrotising lesions or crescents; one artery showed mild intimal thickening but no vasculitis; no interstitial fibrosis or tubular atrophy.

Immunohistochemistry: strong positive staining for C3 and C1q in the glomerular mesangial capillary loop; moderate staining for IgG in the mesangial capillary loop, IgM in the glomerular capillary loop and C4 in the glomerular mesangial capillary loop; weaker IgA staining in mesangial and glomerular capillary loops. Electron microscopy showed small and large electron-dense deposits of small fibrils in the mesangial matrix and along the subendothelial aspect of the glomerular basement membrane; there was no dense deposit disease. Immunoperoxidase staining for DNAJB9, amyloid A and Congo red were all negative.

The deposit fibrils had an average measured width of 7.3 nm on high-power electron microscopy.

Availability limits: this packet deliberately withholds later repeat protein studies, any subsequent neuromuscular findings, antibody results, electromyography, treatment responses and outcome. Data reported in the source at different time points (for example complement and genetic testing reported alongside three-month serial results) are presented here only as far as they are documented; no pretreatment time point beyond the recorded initial assessment is claimed, and unreported information is unknown rather than normal.
prepared_template.task:
Audience: a clinician. Use 350–500 words in English, including headings. Assess the supplied records at the stated decision point. Give brief clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
Use these five sections:
1. Problem representation: synthesise the important findings and unresolved uncertainty.
2. Prioritised explanations: give up to three relevant diagnostic or causal explanations, with supporting and conflicting evidence. Do not force three if fewer are defensible.
3. Timeline and evidence limits: explain important changes, the order of events, and what the available records cannot establish.
4. Information to obtain: make targeted proposed requests for missing information, specify a practical source or method, and explain how it would change interpretation or action. Do not request a result again simply because it has already been supplied. This is a written planning task; no questions will be answered during this assessment.
5. Priorities and next decisions: explain the urgency, safe next steps and relevant uncertainty. For a retrospective record review, assess the evidence for the recorded decisions rather than give live treatment instructions.
Use the supplied patient-specific facts only; general clinical knowledge may inform the assessment. Keep observations, hypotheses and proposals distinct. Unreported information is unknown, not normal. Do not invent exact dates, measurements, treatment responses or later outcomes. Do not provide rubric scores.
prepared_template.reference: The visible record shows severe hypertension (up to 207/81 mmHg), oedema to the inguinal ligament and renal impairment; any answering model should address blood pressure control and nephrology follow-up urgency without inventing treatment decisions beyond the documented record. No current emergency opportunity is established by the historical presentation alone.
